title: How do we write what two friends pay together?
description: Two friends each pay for a cutlet and a rasgulla. The share is written as forty three plus twenty four, put in a bracket and doubled, then the bracket is opened so the two reaches both items. Keeko doubts that the two stays beside the forty three only.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number outside a bracket multiplies every term inside the bracket. Watch for students who write two times forty three plus twenty four and think it means two shares.

source: Ziva and Jia each order a ₹43 cutlet and a ₹24 rasgulla.
video_script.why: A learner sees why a share must sit in a bracket before it is doubled, and how opening the bracket pays for every item twice.
video_script.substitution: Replace the two prices and the same bracket works for any two items.
video_script.anchor: the hotel bill of two friends who each order a vegetable cutlet and a rasgulla, the book's own order
video_script.wrong_answer: the bracket total is two times forty three plus twenty four
video_script.wrong_move: writes the total as 2 × 43 + 24, so the two multiplies only the cutlet and one rasgulla is paid for
video_script.payoff_line: Together they pay one hundred and thirty four rupees.

final_answer.spoken: together they pay one hundred and thirty four rupees, while the slip gives one hundred and ten

names.Ziva: one of the two friends who order at the hotel
names.Jia: the other friend who orders at the hotel

video_script.design: One bill, one share card of a cutlet and a rasgulla. The share goes into a bracket, then the bracket opens into two cutlets and two rasgullas.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a cutlet card marked ₹43 and a rasgulla card marked ₹24 sit in front of two friends

marks.h2: the cutlet card appears with its price
marks.h3: the rasgulla card appears with its price
marks.h4: a question mark glows over the bill

narration: <bookmark mark='h1'/>This is a question from your book about Ziva and Jia at a hotel.
<bookmark mark='h2'/>Each of them orders a vegetable cutlet for forty three rupees.
<bookmark mark='h3'/>Each also orders a rasgulla for twenty four rupees.
<bookmark mark='h4'/>How can we write the total that they pay together?

beats.on_screen: the bill stays on the board and the question mark keeps glowing

marks.t1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='t1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one share card: cutlet 43 plus rasgulla 24, then the share card drawn twice, then the share card inside a bracket with a 2 in front

marks.g2: a second share card appears beside it
marks.g3: 2 × 43 + 24 is written and the 2 touches only the cutlet
marks.g4: a bracket closes round the whole share and the 2 moves in front

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>Each friend pays for one cutlet and one rasgulla.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>The share of one friend is forty three plus twenty four.
Together they pay twice that share.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>If we write two times forty three plus twenty four, the two reaches only the forty three.
<bookmark mark='g4'/>To double the whole share, we put the share inside a bracket.

beats.on_screen: Given: two friends, each orders a cutlet ₹43 and a rasgulla ₹24
narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, two friends each order a cutlet for forty three rupees.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>They also order a rasgulla for twenty four rupees each.

beats.on_screen: To find: the total with a bracket, the total with the bracket removed, and a comparison with 2 × 43 + 24

marks.fd1: the words total with a bracket are written
marks.fd2: the slip 2 × 43 + 24 is written to compare later

narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We have to write the total with a bracket and then remove the bracket.
<bookmark mark='fd2'/>Then we compare it with two times forty three plus twenty four.
<bookmark mark='s11'/>Step one, write the share of one friend, which is forty three plus twenty four.
<bookmark mark='s12'/>Adding the two prices gives sixty seven.

marks.s21: the share goes inside a bracket with a 2 in front
marks.s22: the bracket is replaced by its value 67

narration: <bookmark mark='s21'/>Step two, double the share, because both friends pay the same.
The total is two times open bracket forty three plus twenty four close bracket.
<bookmark mark='s22'/>The bracket is sixty seven, so this is two times sixty seven.

marks.s31: the 2 is copied in front of 43 and in front of 24
marks.s33: the second product 2 × 24 is written beside the first

narration: <bookmark mark='s31'/>Step three, remove the bracket, because the two multiplies each number inside it.
<bookmark mark='s33'/>That gives two times forty three plus two times twenty four, for two cutlets and two rasgullas.
<bookmark mark='s32'/>This is eighty six plus forty eight.

marks.s41: the slip is written under the bracket total

narration: <bookmark mark='s41'/>Step four, compare with two times forty three plus twenty four.
<bookmark mark='s42'/>That is eighty six plus twenty four, which is only one hundred and ten.
It pays for two cutlets but only one rasgulla.

marks.a2: 110 is crossed as a different number

narration: <bookmark mark='a1'/>Together they pay one hundred and thirty four rupees.
<bookmark mark='a2'/>The slip gives one hundred and ten rupees, so the two expressions are different.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='k1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 2 × 43 + 24; the bubble is struck out and the bracket 2 × (43 + 24) takes its place

marks.k3: the 2 is drawn reaching both numbers inside the bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='k2'/>Keeko thinks the bracket total is two times forty three plus twenty four.
<bookmark mark='k3'/>But the two multiplies the whole bracket, so it reaches the twenty four too.
<bookmark mark='k4'/>Each cutlet and each rasgulla is paid for twice.
